author: mindmap-write-lane-c
readerQuestion: How much can I borrow from my 401(k), and what will my loan payments be? [PAA 2/6 on-topic (how much loan can I get from my 401k; $10,000 over 5 years per month), 4/6 off-topic: retirement age, contribution percentage, balance growth; ac 6/44 question completions incl. how much 401k loan can i take, how are 401k loans paid back]

presentation.placement: New spoke page; calculator is section 1, above the explanation
presentation.reason: The answer turns on three reader numbers (vested balance, loans outstanding now and the highest balance in the last 12 months) plus rate and term, which a static table cannot cover.
readerInputs: Highest plan loan balance in the past 12 months
Payments per year (quarterly, monthly or per paycheck)
Loan purpose: general or principal residence

interaction.reason: Statutory cap, repayment and the 5-year and quarterly rules change with each input; the reader cannot read their own cap from a table.

animation.reason: There is no changing quantity worth animating; results update instantly and a 5-row schedule table is the clearer view.

caseDecisions: Retrieved with the exact approved reader question. 8 candidates, none about 401(k) plan loans, short-term real estate loans or ModernWallet readers: they are other Layer3Labs properties, client engagements and a gaming testimonial. ModernWallet's _experience.md has no named-client specifics. Rejected all; no client claim on the page.
exclusions: No TESTED label and no reviewed-by claim: financial service, _experience.md section G excludes it and no product test exists. Internal-modeling wording only.
decisionGap: Readers can find the 72(p) rules in plain language (including our own guide) but still cannot read their own cap: the lesser-of / greater-of formula carries a 12-month highest-balance reduction and loans already owed, and a payment needs a rate and a term. Sampled the 2026-11-14 research pack and DataForSEO read for '401k loan calculator'; no site-wide uniqueness claimed.
finding: In our internal modeling of 26 U.S.C. 72(p)(2)(A), the loan limit is the lesser of $50,000 reduced by how much the highest plan-loan balance in the past 12 months exceeded today's balance, or the greater of half the vested balance or $10,000, and new loans plus loans already owed must fit under it. Vested balances of $15,000, $60,000 and $200,000 with no prior loans give limits of $10,000, $30,000 and $50,000; vested $200,000 with $10,000 owed and a $20,000 12-month peak gives a $40,000 limit and $30,000 of room (subtracting what is owed twice would give $20,000); $200,000 vested with $20,000 owed and a $50,000 peak leaves $0. A $10,000 loan over 5 years paid monthly costs $193.33, $202.76 or $212.47 a month at example rates of 6%, 8% and 10%, with total interest of $1,599.68, $2,165.84 and $2,748.23.
conditions: Federal limits only. The plan document decides whether loans are offered, the rate, fees and how many loans are allowed. A general-purpose loan must be repayable within 5 years (a loan to buy a main home is exempt), with level payments at least quarterly. Rates are reader inputs; the 6%, 8% and 10% examples are not plan or market rates.
whatWouldChange: A plan that bars or limits loans, a term over 5 years on a general-purpose loan, payments less often than quarterly, an additional outstanding loan, or a change to 26 U.S.C. 72(p).
method: Deterministic: limit = min(50,000 - max(0, highest12 - owed), max(vested/2, 10,000)); room = max(0, limit - owed); level payment = P*r/(1-(1+r)^-n) with r = APR/payments per year and n = years*payments per year; schedule run period by period. Python replica of src/lib/401k-loan.ts, checked against the TypeScript engine fixtures.
limitations: No plan fees, no tax on a loan treated as a distribution, no lost investment growth, no plan-specific loan count or rate; payments assumed to start one period after the loan.
counterexample: Subtracting loans already owed from the $50,000 prong as well as from the whole cap double-counts them: vested $200,000, $10,000 owed and a $20,000 peak gives $30,000 of room under the statute but $20,000 under the faulty reading. When owed loans and the 12-month peak exceed the $50,000 prong (owed $20,000, peak $50,000), the room is $0 even with $200,000 vested.
